````markdown
# Voice

How kit's writing sounds. It applies to everything a person or an agent reads: pages, guides, visions, READMEs, tickets and the messages kit shows its users.

## The reader

Write for someone capable who knows programming but not kit, and who can't ask what you meant. An agent reads the same way, only more literally. So be exact, and pair every "don't" with its reason and what to do instead.

## The opening

Open with what the reader came for. An explanation opens with the idea in plain words, a how-to with the first step, and a ticket with the problem and the ask. A reader who stops after the first paragraph should still have the point.

## Length

One subject per page or section. Say each thing once, and cut what a reader would skim: preamble, repetition, and qualifiers that change nothing.

## Truth over time

Text that explains kit describes what is true now, in the present tense, and says plainly what does not work yet. It stays true while the code changes, so it leaves out what goes stale: file paths, counts, dates, versions, owners, tickets and history. Where kit is going lives in a vision, the page that states intent, and is written as intent.

Text about a moment keeps those facts when they are the evidence or the action. That covers a ticket, a review, a report or a brief. A ticket names the failing file; a report dates its numbers.

## Examples

Show an idea working with a small example that uses real values, in the language itself where kit has one. An example teaches more than a description, and more than a pointer to where one lives.

## Words

Explain in everyday words, then give the name the code uses, spelled as the code spells it, so the reader can search for it. Introduce a term in a few words the first time, then keep that name.

## Tone

Plain and calm. Speak to the reader as "you". Let "because" and "so" carry the reasoning. No selling words, no exclamation marks, no "simply". Headings name their topic. Bold marks a word being defined or a warning.

## A worked example

Before:

> Most of kit's own building blocks are declared the same way. The file `docs/src/worldtree/idea/idealic/resource.idea` declares `¶idealic/resource`, titled Resource and described as what every resource is. A collection that cites it, as the market's jobs collection does with `¶jobs §idealic/resource Jobs`, takes on `list`, `write`, `render` and its refusals without writing them.

After:

> Kit describes itself the way it describes everything else: its building blocks are declared in the idea language, not built into the engine. `¶idealic/resource` declares what every resource is. A collection that cites it, as `¶jobs §idealic/resource Jobs` does, gets `list`, `write`, `render` and their refusals without writing any of them.
````
